Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a problem by breaking it down into smaller, identical sub-problems. Each recursive call works on a smaller piece of the problem until reaching a base case—a condition that stops the recursion and returns a concrete result. Without a base case, recursion would continue indefinitely. Classic examples include calculating factorials (n! = n × (n-1)!) or traversing tree structures, where each branch is processed using the same logic as the root.
